bitmap_bit_order: LSB-first within each byte: bit i is byte i/8, mask 1 << (i%8)
description: Conformance vectors for the batch extension to the weir v1 wire protocol: message types PushBatch (0x08) and AckBatch (0x09), the length-prefixed record body, and the positional bitmap reply. Kept apart from wire_v1_vectors.json, which is frozen and is read by decoders that know only message types 0x01..0x05 — such a decoder is CORRECT to reject an 0x08 frame and stays conformant by ignoring this file. 'frame_vectors' are complete frames; 'body_vectors' are bare PushBatch bodies; 'ack_vectors' are bare AckBatch payloads, each with the record count the client sent, which a decoder must be given because a bitmap alone cannot say which batch it answers.

frame_vectors.name: push_batch_three
frame_vectors.notes: PushBatch of three records at Durable durability. The header is a v1 header in every byte but the message type (0x08) and the CRC that covers it — which is the whole claim of additivity: a v1 reader's header parse is unchanged, and only the type dispatch is new.

frame_vectors.name: push_batch_buffered
frame_vectors.notes: PushBatch at Buffered durability. The tier applies to every record in the batch; there is no per-record tier, because a batch shares one ack.

frame_vectors.name: ack_batch_three_all_ok
frame_vectors.notes: The daemon's reply to `push_batch_three`: all three accepted. The durability byte is fixed filler (0x01) exactly as on a plain Ack.

frame_vectors.name: ack_batch_at_the_hard_cap
frame_vectors.notes: The largest AckBatch that exists: 2048 records, 259 payload bytes. This vector is what pins the claim the hard cap was chosen for — 259 is under the 298-byte AckTracked payload, so batching introduces no new largest response and no client gains a new allocation bound. If the cap is ever raised past that, this vector fails.

body_vectors.name: body_three_records
body_vectors.notes: The body carried by `push_batch_three`: version, u16 count, then each record as a u32 little-endian length followed by its bytes.

body_vectors.name: body_single_record
body_vectors.notes: Boundary: N=1. Structurally legal and worth no special case — a batch of one is a batch, and a client that degrades it to a plain Push is making an optimisation, not obeying the protocol.

body_vectors.name: reject_body_truncated
body_vectors.notes: Shorter than the fixed prefix every body has. Rejected before any field offset is interpreted.

body_vectors.name: reject_body_unknown_version
body_vectors.notes: Leading version byte is 0x02. The version leads so the body can grow inside wire v1: a reader meeting a layout it does not know must reject rather than parse a prefix of a layout it has never seen.

body_vectors.name: reject_body_empty_batch
body_vectors.notes: Declares zero records. Not a no-op to be tolerated — nothing legitimate produces one, so it is a framing disagreement and is refused.

body_vectors.name: reject_body_too_many_records
body_vectors.notes: Declares 2049 records in a body of 3 bytes. The rejection must happen on the DECLARED count, before any allocation is sized by it — that is the whole point of checking the cap before the walk, and this vector cannot pass any implementation that reserves first and validates after.

body_vectors.name: reject_body_empty_record
body_vectors.notes: Record 1 declares length 0. The WAB uses a zero payload_len as its end-of-records sentinel and cannot represent an empty record, so this is refused at the edge rather than deeper where the sentinel would be ambiguous.

body_vectors.name: reject_body_truncated_record
body_vectors.notes: Record 0 declares 64 bytes but the body holds 5. The length prefix is peer-chosen and must be checked against what is actually present.

body_vectors.name: reject_body_record_over_the_payload_cap
body_vectors.notes: Record 0 declares 16777217 bytes in a body that carries none of them. The vector is deliberately tiny: it pins the ORDER of the checks, because the cap must be tested before the body is consulted. An implementation that checked `cursor + len > body.len()` first would reject this as TruncatedRecord, which is a different and less informative answer, and would have computed `cursor + len` on a peer-chosen length first.

body_vectors.name: reject_body_more_records_than_declared
body_vectors.notes: Declares 2 records and carries 3. A decoder that stopped at the declared count would silently drop the third; the extra bytes mean the two ends disagree about the body, so the frame is refused.

body_vectors.name: reject_body_fewer_records_than_declared
body_vectors.notes: Declares 4 records and carries 3. The walk ends at the body's end having found fewer than declared.

ack_vectors.name: ack_all_accepted_n3
ack_vectors.notes: The payload carried by `ack_batch_three_all_ok`. Three set bits in one byte: 0b00000111.

ack_vectors.name: ack_all_rejected_n3
ack_vectors.notes: Every bit clear. A clear bit is the WEAK statement: not durable as of this reply, retry, and expect it may nonetheless have been written. Only a set bit inherits the crown invariant.

ack_vectors.name: ack_bitmap_asymmetric_n9
ack_vectors.notes: The vector this file exists for. N=9 with records 0, 2 and 8 accepted encodes as bytes 05 01 under weir's LSB-first convention and a0 80 under MSB-first. Every vector with N<=8, and every symmetric pattern at any N, encodes IDENTICALLY under both conventions and would pass against an inverted implementation — which produces a well-formed frame, valid CRCs and correct length, that reports failures as successes. N>8 forces the byte order to show, and the asymmetric pattern forces the bit order to show. Both are needed; neither alone is sufficient.

ack_vectors.name: ack_exactly_one_byte_n8
ack_vectors.notes: Boundary: N=8 fills the byte exactly, so there are no padding bits and the padding rule has nothing to check. The adjacent N=9 case above is where it starts mattering.

ack_vectors.name: ack_at_the_hard_cap
ack_vectors.notes: The payload of `ack_batch_at_the_hard_cap`: 2048 records, all accepted, 259 bytes.

ack_vectors.name: reject_ack_count_disagrees_with_request
ack_vectors.notes: The payload declares 3 but the client sent 4. A bitmap is the first weir response whose meaning depends on client-held state — an Ack says 'your last record' and an AckTracked carries its own coordinate, but a bitmap is meaningless without knowing which batch it answers. Since ceil(N/8) is not injective (N=1017..1024 all give 131 bytes), the echoed count is the only thing that can catch a desync.

ack_vectors.name: reject_ack_bitmap_too_short
ack_vectors.notes: Declares 9 records but carries one bitmap byte where ceil(9/8)=2 are required.

ack_vectors.name: reject_ack_padding_bits_set
ack_vectors.notes: N=9, so byte 1 holds one used bit and seven padding bits; bit 1 of that byte is set. Ignoring padding would make popcount(bitmap) == N — the obvious way to ask 'did the whole batch succeed' — silently wrong.
